I hit Bitcointalk from the link in the list, and I read post after post after post, and came to the realization that my time would be wasted mining for Bitcoin, that I was too late for that, but that there were ebay alternatives where people were paying the coin for more than what they considered market value because they wanted to spend it on something. Digging through the posts there was a sentiment that was echoed throughout my recently devoured literature. People contributed to the project because they wanted to give money to who and what they wanted without an intermediary (Atlas Shrugged), they wanted to use it without it being anyone's business what they were using it for (1984), that Quality had existed but because of ingrained, repetitive actions could not be realized, and so people would pre-emptively object against that which they feared (Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance), and so, along with mucking my way through the technological understanding of it (and jotting down the pre-requisites I'd need in order to do that) I had nailed down the philosophical understanding of it. It wasn't about what money could do, but what that money represented was freedom, and D'Anconia's speech about money would play over in my head while I saw that this was, in action, what he was talking about. People's misconception about the magic of money and how it can just "appear" rather than something that has work, a value, a Quality behind it. And if it solved that problem, what other problems could it solve? Voting? Governance? Laws? Contracts? In what ways could this faceless, emotionless, distributed machine solve problems of bias, of knee-jerk, of emotional response without removing people's free will? Maybe even problems like mine.

I still starved the next day, but I eventually put the ideas to work for me. I sold salvage electronics people threw out for several coins worth $30 a piece and I held them until next I knew they were worth six times that. I cashed a few out and covered our rent and utilities for a month while my mother tried to secure her first job in 25 years. And so now, a year and a half later, we're doing okay. I learned enough about different development languages to contribute to projects and piece together some of my own. The work within it and the literature that informs it makes me care about these things because for the first time in my life I feel like my own person, that I'm wrestling control over myself, my future, and I've got a decent shot at it. I suppose it's like how at drug rehab places or with Alcoholics Anonymous there's a huge, fertile soil after they've ground everyone down to where they can plant the seeds of religion. I don't think I would've cared about freedom of speech and expression, of decentralized, distributed systems, of a "push" ideology without going through this very specific, very negative, very traumatizing chain of events.

So to get others to stand up for free speech? To shut the fuck up and realize that they all DO have something to hide and shouldn't act like they don't? I don't know. I really don't have any answer other than "lose everything. Resolve to say 'fuck the world' and take back what's yours." But with the way attitudes are and the way we're trained as consumers and how that bleeds over into day-to-day non-consumer tasks and behaviors, subconsciously, I don't know. It looks bleak. I ended up leaving the high school in my new town to do homeschooling, so my day-to-day interactions are rarely with people my own age and are usually with college-aged to 30 year olds in the coffee shop and the hackerspace I attend, and the attitudes with that group are varied; focus on personal protection but definitely no desire to stick their neck out to change anything. They'll bemoan Google but when you keep in contact they give you a gmail address. You know. So my outlook on this is bleak.

This Windows 10 kerfuffle may be the trojan horse necessary to really hit it home. That what you do on the computer isn't private and that your parents have access to what you do. That was a fear of mine, except replace "parent" with "probation officer" and I didn't want them digging through a search history where I had, essentially, my mind splayed out there with everything I was researching and doing or figuring out and didn't want to have to answer for, so I downloaded TAILS and used its clearnet browser to do what I needed, leaving the home computer sparkling and I just cram the USB drive away. But what does a desktop or laptop matter when people are doing stuff with smartphones now and sign their lives away to degenerative, walled-garden systems anyway? Facebook has raised an entire generation to be okay to being a product in exchange to plow fake fields.

A catalyst is necessary, but I don't know what it is.
